slides.say: How many three-digit numbers have a hundreds digit and a units digit whose sum is eight?
So the hundreds digit and the units digit must add up to eight. The tens digit isn't mentioned at all. These questions are not simple, so let's go slowly.
We'll solve it in two different ways. Let's start with the math way, in stages. Three-digit numbers, so three positions, hundreds, tens and units.
Here's a tip that keeps us organized. Above each position, we write how many options it has. Below it, we list what they are.
Like in the lesson, we start with a position that has a restriction, the hundreds digit. Can it be nine? Nine plus even zero is already nine, more than eight. So no.
Can it be zero? No. A number can't start with zero. There's no such number as zero five eight.
So the hundreds digit is one to eight. That's eight options.
Now the units digit. Once the hundreds digit is chosen, the units digit is already decided. It must complete the sum to eight.
If the hundreds digit is three, the units digit must be five. If it's eight, the units digit must be zero. One option every time.
at: If the hundreds digit is three

slides.say: So choosing the hundreds digit really chooses two digits at once.
And the tens digit? The condition doesn't mention it, so it's free. Zero to nine, ten options. A free position can be filled at any point, even first.
Eight times ten times one is eighty.
[pause] Now a quick check, by listing the hundreds and units pairs. The tens digit sits in the middle of each pair.
One and seven, two and six, three and five, four and four.
Five and three, six and two, seven and one, and eight and zero. That's eight pairs.
What about zero and eight? That would start with zero, so it's only a two-digit number. If you count it, you get nine pairs, and nine times ten is ninety. That's choice number one, the trap.
Any of the ten digits can go in the middle of each pair. Eight times ten is eighty again.
at: Eight times ten is eighty again
